title: Composition and Inverse Functions
quickIdea: Compose right to left: (g of f)(x) = g(f(x)). An inverse exists exactly when the function is a bijection, and the inverse of a composite reverses the order.
remember: The composite g after f is defined by (g of f)(x) = g(f(x)), and it is defined only when the image of f lies inside the domain of g.
Composition is associative: h of (g of f) = (h of g) of f. It is not commutative, and g of f and f of g usually differ.
If g of f is injective then f is injective; if g of f is surjective then g is surjective. The other two conclusions do not follow.
A function has an inverse exactly when it is a bijection, and then the inverse is unique.
For a bijection f, f inverse of f is the identity on the domain, and f of f inverse is the identity on the codomain.
The inverse of a composite reverses the order: the inverse of g of f is f inverse of g inverse.
Injectivity of f alone does not give an inverse from B to A; the inverse is defined on the image of f, and it is a function on the codomain only when f is onto.
The identity function is the unit of composition: f of identity = identity of f = f.
A function that is not injective cannot have an inverse, because some output would need two preimages.

example.prompt: f: {1, 2, 3} to {a, b} with f(1) = a, f(2) = a, f(3) = b; g: {a, b} to {x, y} with g(a) = x, g(b) = y. Describe g of f and decide whether f has an inverse.
example.work: Apply f then g: 1 goes to a then x; 2 goes to a then x; 3 goes to b then y. So g of f sends 1 and 2 to x and 3 to y. It is onto {x, y} but not injective. f itself is not injective, because 1 and 2 share the image a.
example.answer: g of f is surjective but not injective, and f has no inverse from {a, b} back to {1, 2, 3}.

gateAngle: Composition questions in GATE are usually decided by cardinality and by the two implication rules: a composite that is injective forces the first function to be injective, and a composite that is onto forces the second to be onto.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x on the integers. Find g of f and its inverse, and check the reversal rule.
variations.answer: (g of f)(x) = 2x + 2 with inverse (y - 2)/2, and f inverse of g inverse gives y/2 - 1 = (y - 2)/2.
variations.why: The composite is a bijection of the integers, so it has an inverse. Computing the two inverses separately and composing them in reverse order reproduces the same map.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: If g of f is injective, must g be injective?
variations.answer: No. f must be injective, but g may collapse elements that f never produces.
variations.why: With A = {1}, B = {a, b}, C = {x}: f(1) = a and g(a) = g(b) = x. Then g of f is injective on the single element, yet g is not injective.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A function f from a 3-element set to a 3-element set is injective. Must it be surjective, and does it have an inverse?
variations.why: On a finite set of equal size an injection uses three distinct images out of three elements, so it is onto, hence bijective, hence invertible.

trap.what: Writing the inverse of a composite in the same order, or assuming that an injective function is invertible on the whole codomain.
trap.why: Undoing a composite means undoing the last step first, which reverses the order of the inverses. And injectivity only makes the map invertible onto its image; surjectivity is what extends the inverse to the codomain.
trap.counterexample: f: {1, 2} to {a, b, c} with f(1) = a, f(2) = b. It is injective, but no inverse function from {a, b, c} to {1, 2} exists, because c has no preimage to send anywhere.

check.question: f and g are bijections on a set A. What is the inverse of g of f?
check.explanation: Composing g of f with f inverse of g inverse returns the identity, because the middle maps cancel: g of (f of f inverse) of g inverse = g of identity of g inverse = identity.
